segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When Dave was turning his life around and trying different things and figuring out what to do next, one of the places he looked was to the Howard Stern Show. And I think that was a really good choice.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I know everybody is not a fan of Howard Stern, but I am. And I think that one of the best things about the show is that it's always been a place where people talk with this kind of brutal and funny honesty about themselves. One of Howard's innovations is that he took the strain of crude, dark, confessional comedy that's always been a big part of stand-up, ever since Lenny Bruce-- Howard figured out a way to turn that into radio, daily radio.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Anyway, to get back to this guy Dave, he loved that about the show. And in 2015, he was a few months sober, in his early 40s, working as a waiter at Katz's Deli in New York City. When he was younger, he'd worked in television, hosting an interview show for college kids but ruined that career with heroin addiction.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Now sober in recovery, he needed a project. And he decided to a podcast about drugs with the feeling of the Howard Stern Show. Like, he remembered the years when comedian Artie Lange was on Howard Stern-- definitely my favorite period of Howard Stern.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When Artie would come on every day. He would talk about his own drug problems. He would tell crazy stories. He would talk in this very real way about the mistakes he was making in his life at that time that he was not able to stop, and Dave wanted to shoot for that. He would co-host the show with his friend Chris who-- he had met Chris years before in rehab.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They would spend hours in rehab smoking cigarettes and talking about the crazy things that they'd done on drugs. That's what they wanted the podcast to be. People'd come on, tell wild drug stories, and-- very important to Dave-- no recovery talk, which Dave found to be sanctimonious and annoying.

segments.text: This show is not necessarily about recovery.

segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.text: If this show is ever about recovery, you got to get somebody else in this spot. I'm out.

segments.text: OK, in case this isn't clear. In these recordings, Dave is the one with the deeper voice and the loud opinions, Chris is the other guy.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And at this point, he'd been sober for nearly two years versus four months for Dave. And all of that gave him a different feeling about recovery and sobriety. He was game to talk about it, but Dave was adamant. Sobriety isn't all that entertaining. And first and foremost, he wanted the podcast to be entertaining.

segments.speaker: Dave

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They were going to call the show War Stories, but there was already a podcast called War Stories. It was about actual war with tanks and guns and stuff, so they came up with Dopey, which really captures the spirit of the show perfectly. As Chris put it, two dopes talking about dope.

segments.speaker: Chris
segments.text: Listen, I am so grateful to be sober. And I'm so grateful to be able to talk about drugs, you know, like in a way where I'm not feeling bad about it. It's not even euphoric recall. It's just funny.

segments.speaker: Dave
segments.text: And I think that's why we got along, 'cause we felt safe doing that with each other. You know, sometimes you feel a little judged with people when you recount funny stuff that's happened to you.

segments.speaker: Chris

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In Dopey, there's going to be no judgment of drug use, past or present. They recorded the first episode on a laptop, no microphone or anything, near a fish tank in Dave's apartment in Manhattan. Maybe you could hear the hum of the tank in that recording. But between this episode, Episode 1 and Episode 143 of Dopey-- just 2 and 1/2 years later-- their lives are going to change drastically.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: By Episode 143, Dopey would sound completely different. In the episodes in between, they chronicle this story where so much happens to them and some others, things lots of drug users face. But because podcasts and radio are so intimate, it all gets documented in the most unfiltered way.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Dave and Chris wanted their show to be just for fun, but it ended up being so much more. Today, we're going to have two stories like this. Stories about a kind of DIY radio-- very different kinds of DIY radio-- but in both stories, it's amateurs inventing how to talk about what it is that they're going through.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And really, both stories are dispatches from two very different battlefields. I know that sounds a little grand, but really this story-- from the opioid epidemic-- and then the other story is from a small town in Syria, in the middle of the war that's going on there. And we hear about life during that war in this way that is much more personal and close up than we usually get. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Stay with us.

segments.text: This was just two weeks after Todd died, so Dave was admittedly on high alert. And by the end of the story, he sees it from Chris's perspective. It's one of those irritating things that happens to people in recovery. You act slightly off one day and everyone assumes you're using again. Dave explains.

segments.speaker: Dave
segments.text: The point of this story-- obviously, you're fine. The point of the story is this is something that addicts have to go through who are using, who are lying. You know what I mean?

segments.speaker: Dave
segments.text: Like, they're covering up their shit or they just got clean and everybody is sure that they're still getting high. Or in your situation-- you know, you're 4 and 1/2 years clean, but like, how do you think somebody should deal with that? Because I bet there's a ton of people listening with very little--

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: The next week they do Episode 142. Normally they record the show on Friday night and Chris puts it online on Saturday morning. But that Friday, Chris gets home from a work trip to Texas and he's too exhausted to record the show. They agree to do it Saturday.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Saturday comes around and Chris is fighting with Annie. He tells Dave he's too upset to record the show. He needs to go to the gym. Then after the gym, he needs another hour.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Dave's getting pissed. He knows The Dopey Nation is expecting an episode. They finally start recording late that night, around 11:00. Chris is lackluster.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Dave's doing most of the work, providing most of the energy. And Chris keeps screwing up and saying things that they later have to bleep out, like where he went on the work trip or his sister's name, or Dave's last name.

segments.speaker: Chris
segments.text: It's amazing that Bob [INAUDIBLE] is driving round and thinks, you know who I should talk to? Dave [BLEEP].

segments.speaker: Dave
segments.text: Why'd you say my last name? Now you have to bleep it.

segments.speaker: Chris
segments.text: Ah, fucking A. Let me put it in my notes. It doesn't even work because we've changed it so much. [BLEEP] Now it's twice. And what else?

segments.speaker: Dave
segments.text: What is wrong with you?

segments.speaker: Chris
segments.text: I don't know. I'm stupid. I can't-- [BLEEP] [BLEEP] --was. I said it once, right?

segments.speaker: Dave
segments.text: Ah, Chris.

segments.speaker: Chris
segments.text: What?

segments.speaker: Dave
segments.text: How are we going to get the show out?

segments.speaker: Chris
segments.text: I'll do it tonight.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Dave's worried that Chris has lost interest in Dopey, that he's too busy with the other things in his life now-- his girlfriend, his job, his doctorate. He starts wondering if Chris is going to quit. And if he does, what will happen to the show? They finally sign off at 1:00 in the morning.

segments.speaker: Chris
segments.text: And stay strong, my brothers and sisters, in and out of recovery. And toodles, I'm going to stop the call recorder. You can stay online. All right?

segments.speaker: Dave
segments.text: Hey, but you don't have to say toodles. It's unnecessary.

segments.speaker: Chris
segments.text: Toodles.

segments.speaker: Dave
segments.text: So hello and welcome to Dopey, the podcast about drugs, addiction, and dumb shit. And I am Dave.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: This is the next episode of Dopey, Episode 143-- a week later.

segments.speaker: Dave
segments.text: For those who aren't on Dopey social media, the worst thing that could have ever happened, happened, and Chris relapsed and died. And here I am alone at my dad's with one microphone plugged into the mixer.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Chris overdosed three days after Episode 142. He'd been secretly using drugs again, probably for weeks. After that last episode they recorded together, Dave and Chris fought.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: First, Chris put the show online without bleeping out Dave's last name. Dave was pissed. He went in and fixed it, but inadvertently inserted 10 minutes of silence into the middle of the episode, which made Chris mad. So that Monday they're fighting over text message all day.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Dave couldn't make sense of what was going on with Chris. He told Chris it was fine if he didn't want to do Dopey anymore. But Chris said no, that wasn't it at all. He loved making Dopey. Dave believed him.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: But meanwhile, Chris was also fighting with Annie. She'd left their apartment and went to stay with her parents. Chris was distraught, crying. He asked Dave to call and check in on him, so Dave called him after midnight and told them he'd check in again in the morning, went to bed.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: He woke up at 6 AM to a text from Annie. She'd sent it in the middle of the night asking Dave if he'd check on Chris. So at 6:30, Dave sent Chris a text message.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: A minute later, Chris wrote back, I'm good. As you like to hear, I'm sleeping, but not totally good. Alive, nothing to worry about. We can talk later. At 10:30, Annie called Dave and told him that Chris was dead.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: In the next few days, Dave had to decide if he was going to do the show that week or ever again. In the 2 and 1/2 years of making Dopey together, they'd never missed a show. Dave thought if he skipped this week, he'd be letting The Dopey Nation down.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: It would be like your drug dealer not showing up. And besides, drug users should know if somebody dies from a drug overdose. So three days after Chris's death, he recorded that episode of Dopey. And he calls Annie.

segments.speaker: Annie
segments.text: Hello?

segments.speaker: Dave
segments.text: Hey, you're on--

segments.speaker: Annie
segments.text: Hey, how are you?

segments.speaker: Dave
segments.text: You're on the show.

segments.speaker: Annie
segments.text: Oh, ha-ha-- hello, everybody.

segments.speaker: Dave
segments.text: How are you feeling?

segments.speaker: Annie
segments.text: Ah, pretty shitty.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: They start to piece together the mystery of Chris's death. Dave had completely misread his behavior. In retrospect, he was probably high on the last episode of Dopey. He was probably high when he made that weird phone call to his sponsor. He was probably even high on the Artie Lange episode.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Dave had been operating off the wrong story-- that Chris wasn't interested in Dopey anymore, but Annie hadn't. She had noticed the strange ways Chris had been acting. He kept taking the dog for walks, for instance, when the dog didn't need to go out.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: He was staying up all night and sleeping during the day. She got suspicious he was using again, so she and Chris's sister arranged for a surprise drug test. On Monday, a guy showed up at their apartment and did a saliva test.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: That night, Annie told him she was going to stay with her parents. Chris left before her mom arrived to pick her up. Now she realized it was because he couldn't wait any longer to get high. Annie slept at her parents' house and went to work the next morning. But soon after, she went home to check on Chris.

segments.speaker: Annie
segments.text: And I don't know if you want me to elaborate on how it was walking into the apartment.

segments.speaker: Dave
segments.text: Yeah, you might as well.

segments.speaker: Annie
segments.text: Or would you rather I not.

segments.speaker: Dave
segments.text: No, you might as well.

segments.speaker: Annie
segments.text: I walked in. The first thing I see is his shoes, so I figure, OK, he's here. And the vape is there, the keys are there, so I look at the couch. He's not on the couch. And I look at the bed, and he's not there.

segments.speaker: Annie
segments.text: And then I [INAUDIBLE] bathroom, I go into the bathroom. He's not there. And that's when I start panicking, and-- and as I walk into the bedroom, on the side of the bed, I found him dead.

segments.speaker: Annie
segments.text: I knew right away he was dead. Everything after that is somewhat foggy. I knew we had Narcan at home, because he always kept Narcan everywhere.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Narcan is a medication that can reverse an opioid overdose. You spray it up a person's nose.

segments.speaker: Annie
segments.text: And I got the Narcan, but I knew it was too late. I just had to do it, because it was like the only thing I could do it at the moment.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Chris had cocaine, Xanax, alcohol, and fentanyl in his system. He was 33 years old. Soon after, a package arrived for him at their apartment. It was filled with drugs-- Percocet, cocaine, crack cocaine, heroin.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Annie scoured the apartment and Chris's car. She found a bunch of drug paraphernalia-- needles, some of which were used, and clean pee he'd ordered online. Also, she found a small medicated patch that wasn't in any packaging.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: She sent a picture of it to Dave. They couldn't be sure, but Dave thought it was probably fentanyl. Annie has a theory about Chris's relapse.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: He had recently injured himself doing a high karate kick to try to impress her. Something in his leg popped, he was in terrible pain.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: The doctor he saw wasn't his regular doctor and she thinks Chris got painkillers, fooled himself into thinking he could just take them for the pain and stop there. If Annie's theory is right, then Chris started using again two weeks after Todd's death and was dead three weeks later.

segments.speaker: Dave
segments.text: I mean, when the news came, I got angry about it. And then the next morning I woke up and-- you know, I felt the day between the last time I had spoken to him. You know what I mean?

segments.speaker: Dave
segments.text: I felt the distance, and I was like, it just felt like it was becoming real. And then this morning I woke up, and I could hear his voice in my head like we were doing the show. I could hear his voice.

segments.speaker: Dave
segments.text: And then I kind of woke up and it was another day since I had spoken to him. And it just-- it's like liquid becoming solid. You know what I mean? And it's like, you move away from this liquid feeling to this cold solid truth that he is never going to come back and it's over.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Dave hangs up with Annie. And now he's got to end this episode of Dopey without Chris for the first time.

segments.speaker: Dave
segments.text: We'll just end it the way we always end it. And we'll say, stay strong Dopey Nation. And I said I would never say this, but Chris is dead, so I'll say toodles for Chris. And we love you. And everybody out there, please try to take care of yourself. All right.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Dave still makes Dopey-- by himself now. He's pulling in bigger guests like the comedian Marc Maron and the rapper Killer Mike. He gets about 6,000 downloads an episode now, but it's not the same show.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Dopey, as the nation knew it, is gone along with Chris. It's not a buddy comedy anymore. It's more of a straight interview show. There are fewer war stories, and when there are, the tone is different. Dave is different.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: There's this one moment in Episode 142, the last episode Dave and Chris did together, that I keep thinking about. Chris had just played a voicemail from a listener named Mike, who tells a story about hiding his pee in the closet of his bedroom. It's not important why. And afterwards, they get into a conversation about whether it's OK to laugh at drug stories.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: In the first episodes of Dopey, Dave was a solid yes on that-- that was the whole point of the show-- but now they've flipped sides. Chris says yes, it's fine to laugh. And Dave says this--

segments.speaker: Dave
segments.text: I think it's funny, but the fucked up thing-- and it might be the end of Dopey, right? Check this out. Like, I just feel like this guy-- he's like everyone's laughing about everything they're doing. And then they can just drop dead.

segments.speaker: Chris
segments.text: But what's the flipside? Morbid reality the whole time until you die?

segments.speaker: Dave
segments.text: No, dude. I think it's funny. I think the urine is funny. I think that shit is hysterical. But it's like laughing on the train tracks and not seeing the fucking train coming. I don't think morbid reality is better. No, of course not. I'm just saying it's sad, you know?

segments.speaker: Chris
segments.text: We laugh on the train tracks, but we have the right to laugh on the train tracks. It'd be much different if someone had never struggled. And the truth is that when we were struggling, the person who would tell a story that was terrifying and laugh at it, might have a better chance at reaching us and getting us to stop than the person who's morbid reality.

segments.speaker: Dave
segments.text: I just feel responsible. I think it's obviously because of Todd's death that when we laugh at stuff, I just want to throw it out there that at any second, Mike could be dead. Because Mike's still using. And there's fentanyl everywhere. And it's killing everybody. That's what I'm saying. How's that?

segments.speaker: Chris
segments.text: Yes, no, of course. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Dave told me, he always thought Dopey was good for him and Chris, for their sobriety. He thought their creation would protect them, but it didn't. Chris is gone. Dopey, it turns out, was its own war story, playing out week by week.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: So now on the show, Dave's mission has changed. The drug stories aren't just in service of a laugh now, they're in service of an urgent message. You could die. Todd died. Chris died. You could die.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Dana Chivvis is one of the producers of our show. The Dopey podcast, you can find it wherever you get your podcasts. Coming up, what happens when you go on the radio and make fun of a militant Islamist group who also happened to run your town, because you're in Syria. That's in a minute, from Chicago Public Radio, when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Each week on our program, of course, we choose a theme, bring you different kinds of stories on that theme. Today's show-- Wartime Radio. People in battlefields of one kind or another, using very DIY grassroots level radio or podcasting to try to make sense of what is happening around them. We've arrived at Act Two of our program. Act Two.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Good Morning, Kafrenbel. So back in my 20s, I was a volunteer reporter at a community radio station in Washington, DC-- WPFW, a great station, that really did reflect the community. DC was 2/3 African-American back then and also had immigrants from all over the world.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And the most popular show on the station, I remember, was the Bama hour. It was a guy named Jerry Washington who would play songs and talk a lot about his niece. There were Caribbean and Central American shows. There was a show made by Iranians who missed the former Shah of Iran. And then another show with Iranians who hated the former Shah of Iran.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: There was a call-in poetry show. Listeners would call in and read their own poems and it was daily. This was a daily call-in poetry show, that in my memory anyway, never seemed to have any kind of trouble getting callers. That's community radio.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Well, this next story is about somebody setting up a station like that-- a community station-- only they're doing it in a war zone, in Syria, in a small town called Kafrenbel. That's Kafrenbel, it's spelled with a K-- in the Northwest part of the country, not far from the Turkish border, rural town, surrounded by olive trees and fig trees, 30,000 people live there.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And for almost eight years now, Kafrenbel's been in a kind of no-man's-land where different factions have fought. And now militant Islamists are in charge. Reporter Dana Ballout heard about the station years before she ever listened to it.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: I crossed paths with the founder of the station back when I was covering the war in Syria for the Wall Street Journal. His name is Raed. Raed Fares. He lives in Kafrenbel.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: We never met in person. I was based across the border in Lebanon, because American press was mostly not allowed in Syria. But when the regime struck a town near Kafrenbel or ISIS was advancing and I needed to know the details from the ground, me and my colleagues would pull out our giant spreadsheet of contacts and go through them. Raed's was one of those names. I'd Skype him to confirm a death count or verify a location, then move on.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Raed was an activist. Before the radio station, he was sort of famous for these banners, these homemade signs written in big block letters on white sheets. He would bring them to protests, post pictures of them on Facebook and Twitter. I always saw them in my feeds. They were witty, like this one from Thanksgiving, a holiday Syria does not celebrate.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Black Friday special offer-- whoever, wherever you are, bring your enemy and come to fight in Syria for free. Limited time offer.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: One of the most viral of these was after Caitlyn Jenner announced her new name Caitlyn, spelled with a C and not a K like the other women's names in her family. Raed gave her this shout-out. Caitlyn, he writes spelling it with a C, we would write Kafrenbel with a C, if it meant, like you, we could be free.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: I knew Raed had his own radio station, Radio Fresh, though I never tuned in back then. But around Thanksgiving last year, I heard Raed had been killed. It hit me harder than I expected.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Saddened by the news, I listened for the first time. You can stream Radio Fresh on SoundCloud. There's hours and hours of programming. Listening through was like reliving the war from the inside. Seeing it in a totally different way from deep in the small town.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: It was incredibly alive, hyper-local, sometimes utterly ordinary, people complaining about their neighbors. But other times, so radical I couldn't believe they got away with it. Here's an example of that. One of the first things I heard-- this satire program called [ARABIC] backstage with the president, where an actor impersonating president Bashar al Assad has made up conversations with an officer in his army.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: That's the actor making fun of the president's lisp, which is very pronounced. He's pretty spot-on.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: I was shocked when I first heard this impression. My knee jerk reaction was oh my god, how did you not go to jail for this? Because in the past, that's what would have happened.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Before listening to Radio Fresh, I had literally heard of two other places in the whole Arab world where anyone had tried to do political satire-- one was Lebanon, where I'm from, and the other Egypt, where for a while til the government ran him out of the country, they had their own version of Jon Stewart. And now there were these guys out of a small town in northern Syria. It completely blew my mind.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: I talked to a bunch of Raed's friends in Kafrenbel. They told me he was always a rebel. Before the uprising against the Syrian regime, he would curse the president in a way no one else dared. He mocked religious figures too.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: His cousin told me this always made people super nervous. Everyone in town knew him as the guy who got kicked out of med school. Raed was a burly guy in his mid 40s, clean shaven, warm eyes, mischievous face. He was sharp, taught himself English, ran a thriving small business.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: One of his best friends, Hadi Abdullah, told me how Raed started the radio station.

segments.speaker: Hadi Abdullah
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: In our mosques, they have loudspeakers.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: These are the speakers for the call to prayer five times a day. At one point, early in the war, the Syrian military showed up in Kafrenbel and started shooting protesters. Raed wanted to get those soldiers to defect.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: So he loaded up a bunch of recordings on a USB stick and had some friends at the mosque blast them over those speakers. Anti- regime slogans like--

segments.speaker: Hadi Abdullah
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: The regime is tricking you. The regime is using you. Regime is killing your family. There are no terrorists here, everybody is civilian here.

segments.speaker: Hadi Abdullah
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: And the idea started from here. And I was like, why am I limiting myself to the mosque only. Why don't I start a radio station, where I could to just talk to people?

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: So shortly after, when Raed found himself meeting with international groups, including the US State Department, he pitched them his idea for a radio station. There are always opportunities in war, and this one would be an unusual chance to push back on the rules, make fun of people they could have never made fun of before, an opportunity to blast out ideas like free speech and democracy to whoever tuned in to 90.0 FM.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: This is a clip from the station's first few weeks on air, August 2013. Radio Fresh was based out of an old government building in Kafrenbel. The studio was done up with shiny purple curtains for soundproofing. There was an ashtray on the table and lots of smoking while they were on the mic.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: The host, who's talking about how to form neighborhood councils, has a thick local accent. One of my favorite things about Radio Fresh-- it sounds rural, slangy, homegrown.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: While I was charmed by the station from the very first clip I heard, the people it was actually made for-- the citizens of Kafrenbel-- many of them were against it in the beginning. Here's Raed himself, on the second anniversary of Radio Fresh, one of the rare times he actually went on air.

segments.speaker: Raed Fares
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: He's saying, in the beginning, there was a lot of talk about how the money for the radio would have been better spent on aid for families in need. People were hungry. They didn't have clean water or electricity.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: It seemed extravagant and frivolous to spend money on a radio show, but pretty early on, the station came up with a program that became indispensable throughout the village. It was called The Observatory. Radio Fresh put 24/7 watchmen in tall buildings to keep an eye out for air strikes.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: As soon as they saw one, they radioed into the station, which would interrupt programming on, say, the nutritional benefits of lettuce--

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: [SIREN]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: --with an air raid siren.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: They're saying, planes are circling over Kafrenbel. Raed's response to the doubters was the radio isn't frivolous. It's about saving lives.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: He's saying, if these airstrike warnings saved even one life, that would be worth the whole cost of the station. Before the observatory, people used to jerry-rig their own version of this alert system-- buying a walkie talkie and eavesdropping on the regime's frequencies.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: It was expensive-- over $100. And parents hated how much the regime thugs would swear and cuss on the frequency. They didn't like that the kids overheard. The Observatory was a clean version for the cost of a basic radio-- $5.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: The air raid warnings-- they were just one of a slew of super practical, you live in a war zone and here's how to survive of programs. There was a medical show that teaches people how to administer first aid. That show has episodes on chemical burns, meningitis in kids, how to treat head injuries--

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Here the host is saying when you think your skull is broken or when you see blood or a clear fluid coming from your ears or nose, get medical help immediately. Radio Fresh had language learning programs in case you had to flee the country.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: They're doing the alphabet in this episode of Teach Me Turkish. More than 3.5 million Syrian refugees have landed in Turkey the last eight years. They also taught French, English. And what I love about these programs is how the people teaching the language are actually not at all fluent in the language they're teaching, but you can hear how hard they're trying.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Dear listeners, welcome to the 11th episode of Teach Me English.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Everyone I talked to about Radio Fresh brought up this one program, called the Complaints Show. It was Radio Fresh's version of a call-in show, except they couldn't actually have a call-in show, because the regime had cut off all the phone lines. So they put up a bunch of little black boxes with a Radio Fresh sticker on them, all around town. People would drop in slips of paper with their answers to quiz shows, their comments and complaints. The host would choose one complaint each week to talk about.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Often, it's very specific stuff. At one point early on, a faction set up shop inside a school building, using it as a police station. Parents were worried about sending their kids to school in a building shared with criminals and thieves. Plus, the police station made the school an easy target for the regime.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Parents told the rebels their concerns, but nothing happened. So they turned to Radio Fresh.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Today, we have a complaint that there is a police station in the same building as a school, and that, the broadcaster says, defies logic. Again, here's Raed's friend, Hadi.

segments.speaker: Hadi Abdullah
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: Some when the people inside the police station heard the episode on the radio, they came right away to us, and they told us, "we're willing to leave the school. Please, tell the families we're going to leave the place. We don't want any trouble against us." And they did. They emptied the police station from all the militants that were there.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: People complained about the price and quality of their bread. Someone brought up their neighbor using a hole in the front yard as a bathroom, while his actual bathroom was broken. The neighbor heard the episode and fixed his toilet. When I first heard the Complaints Show, it felt pretty familiar. We had a similar program in Lebanon, although not quite as small towny as the neighbor's toilet.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: But listening hour after hour, what I realized was that this Complaints Show was doing something besides solving practical local problems. It was also spreading a revolutionary idea, that you could voice your concerns, and hold people accountable, and get results. The guys at the station confirmed this was Raed's original mission for the show. This, in a place where the rules were so recently non-negotiable and you just had to keep your head down and deal with it. The Complaints Show was just one of the many programs, debates, kids shows, series on Islam doing this kind of work.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: One problem people had with the station from the beginning was that it was funded by the Americans, which, in the middle of a war where the US was not being particularly helpful, was not a good look.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: It's true. Almost all the money for the station has come from the US State Department. It's around $40,000 a month these days, which covers the salaries of 53 people. It's a pretty big operation. When listeners accuse the station of being a mouthpiece for the Americans, Raed was happy to address it head on. This is him on the air.

segments.speaker: Raed Fares
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: He says the response is very simple. Have you heard anything on Radio Fresh that sounds like we're supporting the Americans? We're always trying to prod them on the radio, with our banners. We have opinions about them, and we don't hide them. Raed's vision of democracy meant everyone in Kafrenbel had an equal say in what was happening, including women.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: He wanted their voices on the radio too. Although that was such a daring idea for Kafrenbel, even his friend Hadi wondered whether it was possible.

segments.speaker: Hadi Abdullah
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: And I was like, how? He was like, "Easy. You find women, we hire them, we train them."

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: This was bold, because almost no women in the village worked outside the home. They took care of the kids and the homes. That was it. And it was bold because of who was running Kafrenbel at the time. Raed was always offending the local leaders, including just about everyone who was in charge of Kafrenbel over the last eight years.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: First, the Free Syrian Army was offended by a banner, so they came to the radio station and kidnapped two guys. Next, ISIS attacked the station in 2013. A couple weeks later, they shot Raed multiple times, almost killing him. But when Raed was deciding to put women on the air in 2015, two years after Radio Fresh had started, Kafrenbel was run by a new extremist Islamist group, Nusra, al-Qaeda's branch in Syria. Raed knew they wouldn't like this, but he went for it anyway.

segments.speaker: Hiba Abboud
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: That's Hiba Abboud introducing the afternoon newscast. She's now the director of the women's division of Radio Fresh. She talked to me from the women's office over Skype.

segments.speaker: Hiba Abboud
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: I never imagined that I would hear my own voice, or that I would be a reporter. Never.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Hiba was a young newlywed who had just moved to town when she heard that Radio Fresh was recruiting women to go on air. She'd been listening to the radio and was curious what it was like to make it. So she, along with 20 other women, went to the first training. They did icebreakers, spent three days on voice technique.

segments.speaker: Hiba Abboud
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: I don't know if you know this one, but when you put your pen in your mouth, this is a way to open up your voice.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: I did not know this one. Neither did most of the people at This American Life.

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: And how to be as a presenter, and how to take breaths from your belly.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Hiba passed the training and began working at the station, made news shows, programs about women's rights, interviews with local women who had lost their husbands in the war. By the time Raed put Hiba and the other women on the air in 2015, the Islamists in charge of Kafrenbel, Nusra, already hated Radio Fresh.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: The station poked fun at them in all sorts of ways. For being illiterate, hypocritical. One satire depicted their religious police rushing people to the mosque without actually understanding the rules of prayer. Nusra assigned people to listen to Radio Fresh in shifts. They issued regular warnings and threats to the station whenever they heard something they didn't like.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Now Radio Fresh got a lot of warnings for having women on air. Nusra considered their voices shameful, a form of nakedness. Finally, in January 2016, Nusra had had enough. They burst in one morning to shut the station down, broke down the door, faces covered, carrying machine guns. They took everything-- laptops, the transmitter, Hadi's hookah, flash drives. Hiba and the other women watched the Nusra guys ransack the main station from another building, the women's office just up the hill.

segments.speaker: Hiba Abboud
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: And we looked out the window when we heard a lot of noise. So us girls, we just started gathering everything and hiding it. Because we said, you know, they were going to come to us next.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: They quickly rearranged the office to make it look more like a home.

segments.speaker: Hiba Abboud
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: So we were preparing lies, you know, just in case that came in and they started questioning us. And you know, we were going to say like, "Oh, we're just girls here hanging out at her house, and we're just having breakfast together. A morning coffee or a mate.

segments.speaker: Hiba Abboud
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: But they just took the stuff and they left. They didn't even come to us.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Nusra blindfolded Raed and took him to the infamous al-Uqab Prison. They left two armed men at the station to keep anyone from coming in. Every day, Hiba would finish her housework and get dressed to go in for her usual shift, but there wasn't anywhere to go anymore. People started spreading rumors that Radio Fresh was over.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Days passed. Nusra finally reached an agreement with Radio Fresh. They'd let Raed go and return the equipment, under a few conditions. First, that the radio station wouldn't play music. Here's Raed talking about the agreement. In English, actually, in an interview with the CBC.

segments.speaker: Raed Fares
segments.text: They started to say it's forbidden because it's haram in Islam shariah law. In their opinion, it's haram.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Haram, sinful. Nusra had been on Raed's case about playing music for a while. He's cheerfully defiant.

segments.speaker: Raed Fares
segments.text: It was like two years they're asking me to stop playing music, but I refused. Finally, because they attacked the radio station more than three times and kidnapped me like three times--

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Kidnapped me like three times, he's saying.

segments.speaker: Raed Fares
segments.text: Then I stopped playing the music, but I started to play sarcastic thing instead of that. Like animal sounds, like sheep, like birds, hogs, dogs, chicken, and everything.

segments.speaker: Raed Fares
segments.text: [ANIMAL SOUNDS]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Animal sounds. Radio Fresh replaced the jingles leading into each segment with animal noises.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: [ROOSTER CROWING]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: There was a rooster in the morning.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: [BIRDS CHIRPING]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Birds during the day.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: And after dark, of course--

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: [CRICKETS CHIRPING]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: --crickets. The CBC interviewer asked Raed.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: What's the point of that? Why are you doing that?

segments.speaker: Raed Fares
segments.text: When the people hear animal voices, they will ask, "what's going on with Radio Fresh?" And the answer will be, the Islamic armed groups banned the music from Radio Fresh because it's haram. I want them just to think, to use their minds. Is it really haram? You can move the minds. You can move the ideas.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Nusra's other big demand was for Radio Fresh to take women off the air completely. Raed had a creative fix for this one too. Again, here's Hiba.

segments.speaker: Hiba Abboud
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: So we were having a meeting, and he came and he told us that they wanted to transform our voices. You know, now we were going to use something to change our voices from female voices to male, and that you wouldn't be able to tell that it was a female in the first place.

segments.speaker: Hiba Abboud
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: So when we first heard what our voices sounded like, we were laughing. And it was so strange, because we were like, really? This is what people are going to listen to? But after a while, it just became normal, and it literally got to the point where I could tell you which girl was which voice.

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: [CHUCKLING]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: But these days, Hiba just feels annoyed at the voice. And because the voice is so hard to listen to, Radio Fresh reduced how long women speak on the air to a fraction of what it was. By this past fall, the Assad regime had retaken swaths of the country. And in many other places, including Kafrenbel, extremists like Nusra were gaining power. People like Raed, people who didn't want Assad or the extremists, they barely held any ground.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: And finally, around Thanksgiving, Raed was assassinated. I read the news in a tweet, and later heard the whole story. He was in a car with two colleagues from the radio station. It was around noon. A van pulled up next to them and shot and killed Raed and his friend Hamoud Junaid, then drove off.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: While Nusra never claimed responsibility for the assassination, the whole town blamed them. Everyone I knew who had reported on Syria was talking about Raed that day, posting pictures of him, writing that his death was the end of the Syrian Revolution. Because Raed was one of a handful of people in Syria who was still living by the principles of the revolution.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: He was still talking about non-violent resistance and democracy, civil society and freedom. Raed was there from the very first protests in Syria, and stuck by his principles while so many others either died or fell off the train. Now, he too was gone. Hiba got the news over WhatsApp.

segments.speaker: Hiba Abboud
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: At that point, I just wasn't aware of anything anymore. I never thought that moment was going to come. I never imagined that someone like Raed could die. Like, no, he would be-- he would be one of the ones that stayed.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: The funeral lasted three days. Hundreds of people came. There were programs on Radio Fresh remembering Raed and Hamoud, their childhoods, talking to their friends, chatting about their legacy.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: After Raed's death, you can still hear glimpses of Radio Fresh's classic dark humor. They continue to make fun of the president and the local factions. Here's a radio drama about a local guy partitioning his house in Kafrenbel to host refugees.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: But these refugees aren't displaced Syrian women and children. It turns out, no, he wants to host French people fleeing their own country after the Yellow Vest protests, in particular, beautiful French women.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: "Mary, Sonya, Emily sleeping in the streets? Not on my watch." I found the episode hilarious, a sign that Raed's spirit was well and alive at Radio Fresh. I wondered if Raed's friend, Hadi, felt the same way.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Do you still feel that? Do you still feel that at the radio station?

segments.speaker: Hadi Abdullah
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: Yeah, I don't think things will be the same again. I mean, despite all my attempts. Meanwhile, we're trying to manufacture a laugh, but our hearts are not the same.

segments.speaker: Hadi Abdullah
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: I don't wanna be pessimistic, but this is the truth.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: There's a talk that Raed gave two years ago at the Oslo Freedom Forum.

segments.speaker: Raed Fares
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: He opens with footage of the aftermath of a bombing, describing the smell of burned bodies, of guns. The audience is rapt and Raed is gripping. But he also looks very tired of trying to convince these Westerners in peaceful Norway to care about the more than 500,000 Syrians who have died in this conflict and the millions that remain. And yet, there he is. He hadn't given up.

segments.speaker: Raed Fares
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: He ends his speech saying, "There is nothing prettier than a flower that defies death, chaos, and destruction, and instead blooms and radiates hope. Yeah, just like Radio Fresh.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Dana Ballout. She's a filmmaker and a producer at the podcast Kerning Cultures. That's Kerning with a K, Kerning Cultures, which run stories like this one from the Middle East. Last year, Radio Fresh lost its main source of funding when the United States withdrew stabilization aid to Syria. The employees worked without pay for five months. I guess that's what the US government does these days, is just ask people to work without pay everywhere.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Anyway, then they found some temporary funding, but that runs out in March. They're looking for new ways to stay afloat.
